definition: Literary Stories - any narrative arc with beginning, middle, and end

stories.text: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for Ben Kalba Savua. Ben Kalba Savua's daughter saw that Rabbi Akiva was modest and of superior character. She said to him: If I betroth myself to you, will you go to the study hall? He said to her: Yes. She betrothed herself to him in private and sent him away. Her father heard and drove her from his house and took a vow prohibiting her from deriving any benefit from his property. Rabbi Akiva went away and spent twelve years in the study hall. When he returned, he brought twelve thousand students with him. He heard an old man say to her: How long will you remain a living widow? She said to him: If he would listen to me, he would spend another twelve years studying. Rabbi Akiva said: I have permission from her. He turned around and went back to the study hall for another twelve years. When he returned, he brought twenty-four thousand students with him. His wife heard and went out to greet him. Her neighbors said to her: Borrow some clothes and dress properly. She said to them: A righteous man regards the life of his beast. When she came before him, she fell on her face and kissed his feet. His students sought to push her away. He said to them: Leave her, for my Torah and yours is hers.
stories.hebrew_text: רבי עקיבא היה רועה צאן של בן כלבא שבוע. ראתה בתו שהוא צנוע ומעולה. אמרה לו: אם אתקדש לך תלך לבית המדרש? אמר לה: הן. נתקדשה לו בצנעא ושלחתו. שמע אביה, גירשה מביתו ונדר הנאה מנכסיו. הלך וישב בבית המדרש שתים עשרה שנה. כשבא, בא עמו שנים עשר אלף תלמידים. שמע זקן אחד שאמר לה: עד מתי תהיי אלמנה של חיים? אמרה לו: אם שומע לי, יושב עוד שתים עשרה שנה. אמר רבי עקיבא: ברשות ממנה עשיתי. חזר וישב בבית המדרש שתים עשרה שנה אחרות. כשבא, בא עמו עשרים וארבעה אלף תלמידים. שמעה אשתו ויצאה לקראתו. אמרו לה שכנותיה: שאלי בגדים והתלבשי. אמרה להן: צדיק יודע נפש בהמתו. כשבאה לפניו נפלה על פניה ונשקה רגליו. בקשו תלמידיו להדפה. אמר להם: הניחו לה, שלי ושלכם שלה הוא.

analysis.one_sentence_summary: Rabbi Akiva's wife supports him through 24 years of Torah study despite being driven from her father's house, and he credits her when he returns with thousands of students
analysis.reasoning: Complete narrative arc spanning 24 years: Beginning (shepherd Akiva betrothed to wealthy daughter, father disowns her), Middle (12 years study, returns with students, overhears wife support another 12 years), End (returns with 24,000 students, wife greets him, he honors her sacrifice). Rich dialogue, character development, temporal progression, resolution honoring the wife's role.

stories.text: There was a certain poor man who came before Rabbi Nehemiah. He said to him: What do you typically eat? He said to him: Fat meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemiah said to him: Would you be willing to eat lentils with me? He ate lentils with him and died. Rabbi Nehemiah said: Woe to this man that Nehemiah killed him. He should have said: Woe to Nehemiah that he is not worthy to provide fat meat for the poor. Similarly, it happened that Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter was once seen by Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai gathering barley from beneath the hooves of the animals in Acre. He said to her: My daughter, what are you doing? She said to him: Rabbi, provide sustenance for me. He said to her: My daughter, whose daughter are you? She said to him: I am the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion. He said to her: Where did the money of your father's house go? She said to him: Is there not a popular saying in Jerusalem: The salt of money is its distribution to the poor. And some say: The salt of money is reduction through losses.
stories.hebrew_text: עני אחד בא לפני רבי נחמיה. אמר לו: במה אתה סועד? אמר לו: בשר שמן ויין ישן. אמר לו: מי לך להסתפק בעדשים עמי? אכל עמו עדשים ומת. אמר רבי נחמיה: אוי לזה שהרגו נחמיה! היה לו לומר: אוי לנחמיה שאינו ראוי להאכיל עניים בשר שמן. וכן מעשה בבתו של נקדימון בן גוריון, שראה אותה רבי יוחנן בן זכאי מלקטת שעורין מבין רגלי בהמות של עכו. אמר לה: בתי, מה את עושה? אמרה לו: רבי, פרנסני. אמר לה: בתי, בת מי את? אמרה לו: בת נקדימון בן גוריון אני. אמר לה: ממון בית אביך להיכן הלך? אמרה לו: לא משל הוא בירושלים: מלח ממון חסר? ואמרי לה: מלח ממון חסרון.

analysis.one_sentence_summary: Two stories about wealth and poverty: a poor man dies after eating lentils instead of his usual rich food, and Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter is reduced to gleaning barley, illustrating the importance of charity
analysis.reasoning: Two interconnected narratives with complete arcs. First: poor man requests rich food, Rabbi Nehemiah offers lentils, man dies, Rabbi regrets. Second: wealthy man's daughter gleaning barley, Rabbi Yohanan recognizes her, dialogue about lost wealth and charity. Both have setup, dialogue, and moral conclusions about treating the poor appropriately.

stories.text: How does one dance before a bride? Beit Shammai say: The bride as she is. Beit Hillel say: A beautiful and graceful bride. Beit Shammai said to Beit Hillel: If she was lame or blind, does one say about her: A beautiful and graceful bride? But the Torah said: Distance yourself from falsehood. Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai: According to your statement, one who made a bad purchase in the market, should one praise it in his eyes or deprecate it in his eyes? Certainly one should praise it in his eyes. From this the Sages said: A person's disposition should always be pleasant with people.
stories.hebrew_text: כיצד מרקדין לפני הכלה? בית שמאי אומרים: כלה כמות שהיא. ובית הלל אומרים: כלה נאה וחסודה. אמרו להם בית שמאי לבית הלל: הרי שהייתה חיגרת או סומא, אומרים עליה כלה נאה וחסודה? והתורה אמרה: מדבר שקר תרחק! אמרו להם בית הלל לבית שמאי: לדבריכם, מי שלקח מקח רע מן השוק, ישבחנו בעיניו או יגננו בעיניו? הוי אומר: ישבחנו בעיניו. מכאן אמרו חכמים: לעולם תהא דעתו של אדם מעורבת עם הבריות.

analysis.one_sentence_summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debate whether to praise all brides as beautiful, with Beit Hillel arguing through a parable about bad purchases that one should be kind
analysis.reasoning: Dialogue vignette with narrative progression: Beginning (question about dancing before bride, two opinions stated), Middle (Beit Shammai challenges with difficult cases, debate ensues), End (Beit Hillel's parable convinces, concludes with general principle). While no physical action or named individuals beyond the schools, has clear argumentative arc with setup, challenge, response, and resolution.

stories.text: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he said: I need my sons. His sons came in to him. He said to them: Be careful about the honor of your mother. The candle should continue to burn in its place. The table should be set in its place. The bed should be made in its place. Yosef the gardener and Shimon the tailor served me in my life; they shall serve me in my death. He said: I need the Sages of Israel. The Sages of Israel came in to him. He said to them: Do not eulogize me in the outlying towns. Convene the academy after thirty days. My son Shimon is wise. My son Gamliel shall be the patriarch. Hanina bar Hama shall sit at the head.
stories.hebrew_text: כשחלה רבי יהודה הנשיא אמר: צריך אני לבני. נכנסו בניו אצלו. אמר להם: היזהרו בכבוד אמכם. נר ידלק במקומו. שולחן יהא ערוך במקומו. מטה תהא מוצעת במקומה. יוסף הגנן ושמעון החייט ששמשוני בחיי, ישמשוני במותי. אמר: צריך אני לחכמי ישראל. נכנסו חכמי ישראל אצלו. אמר להם: אל תספדו לי בעיירות. התיישבו בישיבה לאחר שלושים יום. שמעון בני חכם. גמליאל בני ישא נשיאות. חנינא בר חמא ישב בראש.

analysis.one_sentence_summary: On his deathbed, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gives final instructions to his sons about honoring their mother and household arrangements, then instructs the Sages about the academy and leadership succession
analysis.reasoning: Deathbed narrative with complete structure: Beginning (Rabbi dying, calls for sons), Middle (instructions about mother's honor and household, calls for Sages), End (final instructions about eulogy, academy, and succession). Multiple characters, dialogue, temporal markers (dying → sons come → instructions → Sages come → more instructions), clear resolution establishing new leadership.

stories.text: The school of Shammai says: The groom is excused from reciting the Shema on the first night. The school of Hillel says: He is not excused. The school of Hillel said to the school of Shammai: We find that Rabban Gamliel married a wife and recited the Shema on the first night. The school of Shammai said to them: It is not a proof, for he was exceptional in this matter and most grooms are not like Rabban Gamliel.
stories.hebrew_text: בית שמאי אומרים: חתן פטור מקריאת שמע בלילה הראשון. ובית הלל אומרים: אינו פטור. אמרו להם בית הלל לבית שמאי: מצינו שרבן גמליאל נשא אשה וקרא קריאת שמע בלילה הראשון. אמרו להם בית שמאי: אינה ראיה, שהוא היה יוצא מן הכלל בדבר זה ואין רוב חתנים כרבן גמליאל.

analysis.one_sentence_summary: Beit Hillel cites Rabban Gamliel reciting Shema on his wedding night as proof against Beit Shammai's exemption, but Beit Shammai argues he was exceptional
analysis.reasoning: Brief debate with embedded anecdote: Beginning (two positions on groom's obligation), Middle (Beit Hillel brings proof from Rabban Gamliel's action), End (Beit Shammai rejects proof as exceptional case). Contains historical anecdote (Rabban Gamliel's wedding night behavior) within legal debate structure. Borderline between legal discussion and narrative, but has progression and resolution.
